newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NAB urges quicker finance sector reform.
newsitem.headline: NAB urges quicker finance sector reform.

text.p: National Australia Bank Ltd managing director Don Argus on Tuesday urged the government to act quickly on finance sector reforms but said some banks may prefer to adopt a protectionist attitude to change.

Argus, in notes released here for a speech to the Australia/Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said he had been insistent in presentations to government and industry that Australia needed to maintain an adequate pace of reform.
"I have expressed a concern that some banks may prefer to adopt a quasi protectionist attitude in a myopic effort to avoid the full impact of the globalisation of our industry," he said.
Last week Argus told a function in Adelaide that the federal government's block on big bank mergers was also myopic and a farcical attempt to hold off industry rationalisation.
NAB, Australia's biggest bank, is seen as the most likely predator if big-bank mergers are allowed by the government.
After the release of the Wallis enquiry into Australia's finance industry in April, the government said it wanted to see more competition develop in the bank sector before allowing big-bank mergers.
Argus said NAB was arguing for an open, transparent, fully competitive finance industry and that this approach was consistent with the government's stated aims of reducing protectionism.
Australia needed to resolve a number of domestic issues in order to progress its business relationships with Asian countries, Argus said.

He said that although Australia was experiencing economic growth and its public facilities were world class, there was a perception that the benefits were not equally distributed, especially to young people due to chronic unemployment.
"It is this internal paradox - the perception of national failure at a time of relative international success, that is complicating Australia's engagement with Asia," Argus said.
Argus said Australia had to address the need for a clear articulation of its values, priorities and sense of identity.
"Australia needs to have a clear understanding of how its relationship with Asia fits with its relationship with other regions and nations," he said.
Argus said Australian companies also needed to improve their knowledge of contemporary Asian politics, economics and culture.
